metadata.summary: Background: The molecular mechanisms underlying heart failure (HF) following myocardial infarction (MI) (HF-MI) remain incompletely understood, and whole-transcriptome profiling studies hold significant promise for disease prevention and treatment. Methods: Whole-transcriptome sequencing was performed on post-MI patients with and without HF to analyze differentially expressed mRNAs, lncRNAs, and circRNAs, along with functional enrichment analysis. Co-expression networks linking lncRNA-mRNA and circRNA-mRNA pairs, as well as ceRNA networks involving lncRNA-miRNA-mRNA and circRNA-miRNA-mRNA interactions, were constructed for differentially expressed (DE) RNAs. Key lncRNAs were validated by RT-qPCR. Transcriptional factor-lncRNA networks were constructed, and key relationships were verified using RIP-PCR. Results: Patients with HF-MI exhibited marked elevation of NT-proBNP and significant reduction in LVEF%. Transcriptome-wide analysis revealed 228 DE-mRNAs, 700 DE-lncRNAs, and 1188 DE-circRNAs in HF-MI compared to non-heart failure patients (NHF-MI). Construction of the ceRNA network identified hsa-miR-6089 and hsa-miR-6771-5p as key miRNAs in the lncRNA-miRNA-mRNA network, while hsa-miR-1207-5p and hsa-miR-10392-3p were key miRNAs in the circRNA-miRNA-mRNA network. PVT1, SNHG5, TTN-AS1, HCP5, and OIP5-AS1 were identified as the five key DE-lncRNAs, with PVT1/SNHG5 showing upregulation and TTN-AS1/HCP5/OIP5-AS1 exhibiting downregulation. The transcription factor-lncRNA network primarily involves GLIS3-HCP5 and ZNF135-PVT1, with validated associative interactions. Conclusion: This study systematically mapped the regulatory network of HF-MI, revealing the roles of the GLIS3-HCP5 and ZNF135-PVT1 regulatory axes in HF-MI, thereby providing a basis for exploring novel therapeutic strategies.

observations.text: High levels of IL-18 have been causally implicated in IBD risk and may represent a unique mechanism driving IBD yet to be therapeutically targeted. To identify individuals predisposed to increased levels of IL-18, we implemented a polygenic approach to predict IL-18 plasma protein levels. Using a dataset with over 50,000 individuals with both genetic and plasma protein levels from Olink, we developed a 27 SNP polygenic score that predicts IL-18 levels and IBD risk. Further, we identified a threshold to classify patients as  IL-18 High using a data-driven approach that optimized prediction of both IL-18 and IBD risk. We show that [~]30% of the overall IBD patient population is  IL-18 High, meaning a genetic predisposition towards higher protein levels. The IL-18 PGS and corresponding threshold have the potential to identify IBD patients with IL-18-driven IBD that may respond more effectively to a therapy targeting this mechanism.

BackgroundAttentional control declines with normal aging, yet the role of modifiable lifestyle factors in accelerating this decline remains incompletely characterised in large, diverse populations. We examined associations between four modifiable risk factors (smoking intensity, alcohol binge drinking, social satisfaction and blood pressure) and sustained attention performance in 13,866 adults drawn from the All of Us Research Program.

MethodsCognitive performance was assessed using the Gradual-Onset Continuous Performance Task (GradCPT). A composite cognitive efficiency score was derived via principal component analysis of four GradCPT metrics: d' (perceptual sensitivity), response criterion, median reaction time and reaction time variability. Associations between cognitive efficiency and each risk factor were examined using multiple linear regression adjusted for age, sex and race/ethnicity. Effect sizes were expressed as age-equivalent years of cognitive aging (age-equivalent years = regression coefficient for the risk factor divided by the regression coefficient for age) to aid clinical interpretation.

ResultsGradCPT performance declined progressively with age (p < 0.001). Social satisfaction emerged as the strongest lifestyle predictor: low social satisfaction was associated with approximately 5.8 additional age-equivalent years of cognitive aging relative to high social satisfaction. Smoking showed a dose-response pattern, with heavy smokers (> 20 cigarettes/day) exhibiting an approximately 5-year age-equivalent deficit versus never-smokers. Stage 2 hypertension showed a modest, non-significant negative association. Binge drinking showed limited significant associations, likely complicated by survivor and abstainer biases. Bootstrapped analyses of combined exposures showed that combinations of risk factors, particularly those involving low social satisfaction, produced larger cognitive deficits than expected under an additive model.

ConclusionsThese findings support an interactive rather than a purely additive model of lifestyle-related cognitive vulnerability and highlight the GradCPT as a subclinical measure of attention-based cognitive risk in non-clinical populations.

metadata.summary: Myocardial infarction (MI) causes cardiomyocyte loss and fibrotic scar formation, disrupting electrical communication and impairing cardiac function. Conductive hydrogels have been studied to reconstruct an electroactive microenvironment for the infarcted myocardium, yet their regenerative effect is limited by the impaired function of surviving cardiomyocytes. Here, we developed a mechanoelectrically active and paintable hydrogel capable of converting cardiac motion into localized electrical stimulation to repair infarcted myocardium. The paintable nature of the hydrogel enables easy application onto irregular epicardial surfaces using a customized brush, while subsequent photocrosslinking allows selective adhesion of the hydrogel to only epicardial surfaces, not to surrounding tissues. Under cyclic loading and in contracting cardiac organoids, the hydrogel generated physiologically relevant electrical potentials, demonstrating efficient deformation-induced charge generation. In a rat MI model, the hydrogel providing electrostimulation alleviated ventricular wall thinning and fibrosis, promoted neovascularization and M2 macrophage polarization, and improved cardiac function. Transcriptomic analysis further revealed upregulation of genes involved in myocardial contraction and energy metabolism. As such, our study offers a minimally invasive and clinically translatable approach for cardiac repair and other tissue applications.

metadata.summary: This study generated a transcriptome-wide resource of peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) from two clinical groups: subjects with hyperuricemia (HUA, n=15) and subjects with coronary artery disease together with hyperuricemia (CHD_HUA, n=15). Total RNA was extracted from PBMC and poly(A)+ mRNA was enriched with oligo(dT) magnetic beads. Strand-specific libraries were constructed using dUTP incorporation and UDG second-strand digestion, and paired-end 150 bp sequencing was performed on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000. Clean reads were aligned to the Homo sapiens reference genome with HISAT2, and transcripts were assembled and quantified with StringTie. Gene-level raw read counts and FPKM values for all 30 samples are provided as processed data, together with the paired-end FASTQ files. The dataset is intended to support investigation of transcriptional differences between hyperuricemia and coronary artery disease with hyperuricemia.

PurposeTo evaluate a medical vision-language foundation model fine-tuned on thyroid ultrasound images, with or without the radiologists structured descriptors, against expert-rated EU-TIRADS for the classification of thyroid nodules as benign or malignant.

Materials and MethodsThis retrospective study included nodules that underwent ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration (FNA) between January 2019 and August 2025 in two Tunisian centers, with consecutive recruitment, together with a selection of images from an international public dataset. Of 1,580 nodules, 1,456 (272 malignant; 1,280 patients) with an interpretable cytological or histological reference standard were allocated at patient level to training (n = 942), validation (n = 258) and a test set sealed before training (n = 256; 51 malignant). MedGemma 1.5 4B was fine-tuned with low-rank adaptation under four input configurations: the image with nodule biometry, with or without age and sex (A, B); A with chain-of-thought supervision (C); and A plus the eleven qualitative descriptors of the radiologists structured report (D). The EU-TIRADS category was never a model input. Areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROCs) were compared with DeLongs test and a prespecified non-inferiority margin of 0.05; EU-TIRADS [≥] 4 was the prespecified comparator, with [≥] 5 as a sensitivity analysis.

ResultsConfig D reached an AUROC of 0.953 (95% CI 0.909-0.976), versus 0.948 (0.894-0.972) for EU-TIRADS (difference +0.004, 95% CI -0.016 to +0.025), which met the non-inferiority criterion; Configs A-C, without the qualitative descriptors, reached 0.883-0.892 (Holm-adjusted p = 0.045 versus EU-TIRADS). At [≥] 4, EU-TIRADS had a sensitivity of 98.0% and produced 94 false positives among 205 benign nodules; at a threshold fixed on validation data, Config D reclassified 72 of them as negative while missing two additional cancers. Against EU-TIRADS [≥] 5 (sensitivity 92.2%, specificity 95.1%), Config D at its native threshold (88.2%, 94.1%) did not classify more nodules correctly (McNemar p = 0.22), and at its two other thresholds it classified fewer nodules correctly (p = 0.004 and 0.007). Raw probabilities were miscalibrated (expected calibration error 0.117 for Config D), and Platt scaling within the test set reduced this error to 0.019-0.040.

ConclusionGiven the ultrasound image together with the radiologists structured descriptors, the fine-tuned model matched expert EU-TIRADS discrimination and, against the [≥] 4 threshold, reclassified most false positives as negative, a gain concentrated in category 4 and based on only three cancers in category 4. It is best positioned as a report-standardizing second reader in the EU-TIRADS 4 gray zone, pending prospective external validation.

Summary StatementA fine-tuned medical vision-language model given the ultrasound image and the radiologists structured report matched expert EU-TIRADS discrimination of thyroid nodules and would have deferred most aspirations of benign category 4 nodules, at the cost of one or two missed category 4 cancers depending on the threshold, based on only three cancers in category 4.

Key PointsO_LIOn a test set of 256 thyroid nodules sealed before training, the model given the ultrasound image and the radiologists 16-field structured report reached an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.953, non-inferior to expert EU-TIRADS (0.948).
C_LIO_LIAgainst EU-TIRADS 4 or higher, the model reclassified as negative 72 of the 94 false-positive nodules at a threshold fixed on validation data, at the cost of two additional missed cancers.
C_LIO_LIAdding the radiologists qualitative descriptors to the image raised the area under the curve from 0.892 (Config A) to 0.953, and Platt scaling reduced the calibration error of the model from 0.117 to 0.019-0.040.

Hyodeoxycholic acid (HDCA), a natural secondary bile acid, plays key roles in metabolic homeostasis, yet its direct cardioprotective effects in obesity-related cardiac injury remain unclear. HDCA also bound PIK3CA to inhibit PI3K-AKT-mediated inflammation. In 3D cardiac spheroids, HDCA alleviated lipotoxic injury. metadata.summary: Laminopathies comprise a diverse array of phenotypes that involve multiple organs and are caused by mutations in the LMNA gene, which encodes nuclear envelope protein lamin A (LMNA). Cardiac involvement is a prominent feature and a major cause of mortality and morbidity in laminopathies. LMNA interacts with chromatin through lamin-associated domains (LADs) and regulates gene expression. The role of the LMNA in regulating chromatin structure and gene expression in cardiac myocytes is unknown.  We conditionally deleted the Lmna gene specifically in cardiac myocytes in the mouse, isolated the LMNA-deficient cardiac myocytes, and characterized genomic structure and function at two levels: first, by identifying and characterizing the genome-wide CTCF binding sites by a CUT&RUN assay; and second, the chromatin conformational changes by HiC.  To determine the role of LMNA in genome organization and gene expression we integrated CTCF binding, LAD, Hi-C data with the gene expression (RNA-seq), and DNA double-stranded breaks (DSBs), determined by END-Seq, in cardiac myocytes.  Compared to wild-type (WT) myocytes, LMNA deficiency increased genomic occupancy of CTCF , predominantly outside of the constitutive LADs (cLADs), and increased gene expression at the CTCF binding sites. Likewise, DSBs were highly enriched at the CTCF binding sites. However, only a small fraction of the chromatin compartments was shifted in the LMNA-deficient cardiac myocytes. LMNA-deficiency changed the organization of one-third of the topologically-associated domains (TADs). The changes were characterized by the merger of 2 or more TADs (60%), mainly in the non-LAD regions, splitting (30%), and shifting boundaries (10%). Reorganization of TADs, however, did not directly affect gene expression or the prevalence of DSBs. A remarkable effect of the LMNA deficiency was on chromatin loops, as it led to a gain of ~ 600 and a loss of ~1000 loops, whose boundaries were enriched in the CTCF binding sites. The changes affected the transcript level of ~25% of the differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in the LMNA-deficient cardiac myocytes. The gain of the loop was associated with increased gene expression, whereas the loss of the loop had the opposite effect. A multivariate analysis showed that differential CTCF  binding  (largest), loops, and cLADs affected the transcript levels of the DEGs, whereas TADs and chromatin compartments appeared to act in concert with these factors  rather than as independent determinants.  In conclusion, LMNA regulates chromatin structure like TADs its role in  gene expression is mediated mainly through CTCF, cLADs, and loops,. The findings provide insights into the molecular pathogenesis of cardiac involvement in the diverse array of phenotypes in laminopathies.

metadata.summary: Truncating variants in desmoplakin (DSP) are a leading cause of arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, a severe heart muscle disease characterized by fibrosis and life-threatening arrhythmias. Desmoplakin anchors the junctions that hold heart muscle cells together to the internal cytoskeleton, enabling the heart to withstand the force of each contraction. No targeted therapy exists, and DSP is too large for conventional gene replacement. Here we show, in explanted human hearts and in human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes, that truncating DSP variants reduce desmoplakin RNA and protein, and that the resulting haploinsufficiency renders cardiomyocytes vulnerable to cell–cell adhesion failure under contractile stress, preceded by disruption of the cell membrane. Lowering contractile force with the myosin inhibitor mavacamten prevents this failure. Circumventing the size of DSP, CRISPR-based transcriptional activation of the endogenous gene restores desmoplakin expression and rescues adhesion. Haploinsufficiency is therefore the primary defect in DSP cardiomyopathy, and transcriptional activation offers a therapeutic strategy.

metadata.summary: Diabetic cardiomyopathy is a clinical condition of ventricular dysfunction, with obesity and insulin resistance as the primary risk factors. Under this condition, the heart accumulates fatty acids and encounters lipotoxicity, which impairs cardiac insulin sensitivity and leads to cardiomyopathy. Angiotensin-(1-9) is a peptide of the counter-regulatory axis of the renin-angiotensin system with cardioprotective effects in myocardial infarction. However, its role in diabetic cardiomyopathy is unknown. To explore the role of angiotensin-(1-9), we first induced lipotoxic stress in the heart by high-fat diet (HFD) feeding in mice. Angiotensin-(1-9) was then administered for four weeks using osmotic mini-pumps. Cardiac function was assessed by, and insulin sensitivity was evaluated in tissues after a bolus of insulin injection. Moreover, lipotoxic stress in vitro was modeled by high glucose medium plus palmitate in neonatal rat ventricular myocytes (NRVMs). We show that angiotensin-(1-9) improves myocardial function and reverts pathological cardiac remodeling in mice. Moreover, angiotensin-(1-9) enhances whole-body glucose tolerance and reduces homeostatic model assessment of insulin resistance (HOMA-IR). We next demonstrate that angiotensin-(1-9) increases insulin sensitivity in the heart and skeletal muscle but not in adipose tissue or the liver. Mechanistically, angiotensin-(1-9) does not affect insulin signaling in cardiomyocytes at baseline, while it significantly improves insulin action under lipotoxic stress through AT2 receptor (AT2R) and PKA. These findings demonstrate that angiotensin-(1-9) improves cardiac function under metabolic challenge and promotes insulin signaling in cardiomyocytes under lipotoxicity, which may shed light on the therapeutic exploration against diabetic cardiomyopathy.

metadata.summary: Background: Reactive oxygen species are increased across most pulmonary hypertension (PH) etiologies, resulting in increased reactive lipid dicarbonyls, which form protein adducts and impair mitochondrial function. We hypothesized that reducing reactive lipids would reduce right ventricular systolic pressure (RVSP) and improve cardiac function by eliminating protein-lipid damage feedback loops. Methods: We used 2-hydroxybenzylamine (2-HOBA) to scavenge reactive lipids in three complimentary mouse models of PH: AKR-high fat diet (HFD, metabolic stress), LNAME-HFD (cardiometabolic syndrome), and pulmonary artery banding (PAB, load stress). Cardiac function was measured by echocardiography and catheterization. RV energy metabolism was determined by oxygraphy. Mass spectrometry analyzed lipids and ceramides; O-link and RNA-Seq evaluated proteomic and gene expression in lungs, RV, and LV. Results: Reducing reactive lipids with 2-HOBA resulted in a ~10% reduction in RVSP, reduced diastolic dysfunction, reduced plasma lipids and ceramides, and normalized RV fatty acid oxidation that was severely impaired in the AKR-HFD and PAB models. Proteomic and RNA changes in the lungs, RV, and LV suggested reduced oxidative damage and inflammatory signaling and altered developmental and actin organization signaling; these changes are plausibly associated with the improved adaptation. Some changes were sex specific, including a 4x higher cardiac fatty acid content in males than females. Conclusions: Reactive lipid scavenging improves cardiac metabolic and diastolic function and pulmonary vascular resistance through restoration of mitochondrial function and reduced oxidative protein damage. The magnitude of hemodynamic improvement combined with substantial diastolic function improvement suggests clinical potential, particularly for PH patients with metabolic comorbidities.

BackgroundLiver diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) often shows signal loss in the left lobe due to cardiac pulsation, known as the pulsation artifact.

PurposeThis study was conducted to turn this bug into a feature. We hypothesized that the pulsation artifact, caused by mechanically transmitted waves, is influenced by tissue stiffness and, thereby, indicative of cirrhosis in the left liver lobe. Thus, we evaluated the potential of DWI pulsation artifacts to detect liver cirrhosis.

Study typeThis study included both retrospective patients and prospective healthy volunteers.

Study populationThirteen healthy volunteers, 16 patients with cirrhosis (Ishak 5 or 6), and three patients without cirrhosis (Ishak 0, 1, or 2) were included.

Field Strength/SequenceImaging was performed at 1.5 T and 3 T using echoplanar DWI of the liver with two b-values, b50 = 50 s/mm{superscript 2} and b800 = 800 s/mm{superscript 2}.

AssessmentAfter manual segmentation of the left and right liver lobes, 18 first-order features were extracted from b50 and b800 images. We assumed the pulsation artifact was predominantly present in the left liver lobe in the b800 images. Thus, we computed the ratios of the intensity-normalized b800 features obtained from the left and right liver lobes. Additionally, we performed an intensity normalization to address the sometimes different signal intensities of left and right liver lobe. Then, we conducted a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis to differentiate cirrhotic from non-cirrhotic livers.

Statistical testsROC analysis and leave-one-out bootstrapping were applied, both yielding area under the curve (AUC) values.

ResultsLeft liver pulsation artifacts were more pronounced in non-cirrhotic livers and largely absent in cirrhotic livers. The first quartile feature, i.e. the first quartile of the normalized signal, best distinguished cirrhotic from non-cirrhotic livers (AUC = 0.95; 95% confidence interval 0.87 - 1.00).

Data conclusionThe left liver DWI pulsation artifact reflects liver stiffness and could serve as a simple, intrinsic marker of liver cirrhosis. Analysis of the signal magnitude can differentiate cirrhotic from non-cirrhotic livers.

metadata.summary: Truncating variants in desmoplakin (DSP) are a leading cause of arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, a severe heart muscle disease characterized by fibrosis and life-threatening arrhythmias. Desmoplakin anchors the junctions that hold heart muscle cells together to the internal cytoskeleton, enabling the heart to withstand the force of each contraction. Lowering contractile force with the myosin inhibitor mavacamten prevents this failure. Circumventing the size of DSP, CRISPR-based transcriptional activation of the endogenous gene restores desmoplakin expression and rescues adhesion. Haploinsufficiency is therefore the primary defect in DSP cardiomyopathy, and transcriptional activation offers a therapeutic strategy.

observations.text: Automated extraction of molecular interactions from scientific literature has outpaced the development of systematic methods for integrating this information with curated models and knowledge graphs. Here we present VIOLIN (Versatile Interaction Organizing to Leverage Information in Networks), a configurable, attribute-aware reconciliation framework that formally compares newly extracted interaction lists against structured baseline graphs. VIOLIN classifies each interaction as a corroboration, contradiction, flagged case, or extension, and supports configurable attribute inclusion strategies and mismatch semantics to adjust reconciliation strictness. We evaluate VIOLIN using interaction lists generated by two traditional NLP systems (REACH, INDRA) and two large language models (GPT-4.1, Llama 3) across multiple literature corpora and structurally distinct baseline graphs. Across all conditions, reconciliation outcomes were stable and interpretable, with extensions dominating and corroboration-contradiction balance reflecting intrinsic structural relationships between baseline graphs and extracted evidence. Sensitivity analyses demonstrate that attribute inclusion and classification scheme selection shift category boundaries predictably. Benchmark evaluations confirm high algorithmic correctness and alignment with expert curation. VIOLIN is publicly available as a Python package and through web-based interface (https://nmzlab.github.io/Tools-UI).

observations.text: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) is among the most prevalent mental disorders. Associations between resting-state fMRI functional connectivity (FC) and AUD have been reported but rarely replicated. In this preregistered study, we investigated the extent to which FC predicts alcohol consumption, as measured by the AUDIT-C score, in a large sample of non-treatment-seeking alcohol consumers (N = 739), including 528 participants with varying degrees of AUD severity. To optimize performance, we compared kernel ridge regression (KRR) trained directly on this sample with transfer-learning models based on multilayer meta-matching embeddings, from which we derived data-driven relevance maps at the connection, region, and network levels. We tested split-half reliability, reproducibility across cohorts, and outcome specificity of the relevance maps. Both models predicted AUDIT-C scores moderately but significantly (r {approx} 0.15). Meta-matching did not outperform KRR in prediction. Relevance maps showed limited split-half reliability, consistent with the modest predictive performance, but reproduced moderately well across two independent cohorts. These maps indicate reduced connectivity among limbic regions, the anterior middle temporal gyrus, the dorsomedial prefrontal cortex, and dorsal attention network regions. In contrast, hypothesized hyperconnectivity patterns involving the striatum, anterior cingulate cortex, and precuneus were less reliable and mostly non-significant. Overall, our findings suggest that resting-state FC contains reproducible but weak signals related to alcohol consumption. Transfer learning improved relevance-map reliability but not prediction performance and reduced outcome specificity. These results support the utility of interpretable machine learning for identifying connectivity patterns related to drinking behavior, while also highlighting current limitations in its predictive power.

observations.text: Epigenetic studies of psychiatric and neurological disorders rely largely on peripheral tissues, yet where peripheral DNA methylation (DNAm) reflects the brain remains unclear. We generated a paired brain and peripheral DNAm dataset from 148 donors in three cohorts and combined it with five published cohorts for consensus brain-peripheral correlations. By cross-validation across cohorts, we defined brain epigenome shared sites (BrESS), more than 100,000 CpGs per tissue at which peripheral DNAm reproducibly predicts brain DNAm. BrESS lay at promoters active in both brain and periphery and in housekeeping genes, and most were not explained by genetic effects. BrESS did not contribute to the heritability of seven disorders, and CpGs from epigenome-wide association studies of these disorders were not enriched at BrESS. Peripheral DNAm reflects the brain mainly in a regulatory compartment shared across tissues, outside which disease signals largely lie, and BrESS separate peripheral signals attributable to the brain from others.

Key PointsO_ST_ABSQuestionC_ST_ABSWhich candidate plasma proteins are associated with cognitive performance across multiple domains in older adults from the Democratic Republic of Congo?

FindingsIn this cross-sectional study of 779 participants, higher MME was associated with better language, global cognition, and delayed memory; higher NEFL was associated with poorer global cognition and delayed memory; and ENO2 was associated with delayed memory. No p-tau217-based measure remained significant after within-outcome multiple-testing correction.

MeaningPlasma markers most closely associated with cognitive phenotype may differ from biomarkers optimized for Alzheimer pathology detection, underscoring the need for population-specific biomarker evaluation.

ImportanceBlood-based proteomic biomarkers may support scalable dementia research, but their associations with cognitive phenotype remain poorly characterized in sub-Saharan African populations.

ObjectiveTo examine associations between selected plasma proteins and multidomain cognitive performance in older adults in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

DesignCross-sectional secondary analysis of baseline data from the Etude du Vieillissement Cognitif et de Demence en Republique Democratique du Congo (EVCD-RDC), with participant recruitment and data collection from July 2024 through September 2025.

SettingCommunity-based prospective cohort in Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of Congo.

ParticipantsThe analytic sample included 779 participants: 143 cognitively unimpaired, 218 with mild cognitive impairment, 203 with Alzheimer disease, and 215 with other dementia. Median age was 73 years (IQR, 70-78); 495 participants (63.5%) were female and 284 (36.5%) were male.

ExposuresPlasma abundance of 10 candidate proteins measured using the NULISAseq CNS Disease Panel 120. Candidates were selected from an earlier panel-wide analysis based on cognitively unimpaired vs Alzheimer disease discrimination and false-discovery-rate-adjusted significance.

Main Outcomes and MeasuresSeven cognitive outcomes spanning global cognition, language, working memory, learning, delayed memory, mental abstraction, and problem solving. Separate linear regression models adjusted for age, sex, current smoking, education, and estimated glomerular filtration rate. Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate correction was applied within each cognitive outcome across the 10 proteins.

ResultsEighteen protein-cognition associations were nominally significant, and 6 remained significant after correction. Higher MME was associated with better language ({beta}=0.143; 95% CI, 0.074-0.212), global cognition ({beta}=0.225; 95% CI, 0.071-0.379), and delayed memory ({beta}=0.312; 95% CI, 0.106-0.519). Higher NEFL was associated with poorer global cognition ({beta}=-0.700; 95% CI, -1.080 to -0.319) and delayed memory ({beta}=-0.773; 95% CI, -1.283 to -0.263). Higher ENO2 was associated with better delayed memory ({beta}=0.560; 95% CI, 0.184-0.937). No p-tau217-based measure remained significant after correction.

Conclusions and RelevanceMME and NEFL showed the most consistent associations with cognitive performance, whereas p-tau217-based measures did not survive multiple-testing correction. Biomarkers optimized for Alzheimer pathology detection may differ from those most closely associated with cross-sectional cognitive phenotype, supporting population-specific evaluation of plasma proteomic markers.

Consistently, RNA-binding-deficient MLP mutants exhibit impaired interactions with cytoskeletal proteins and reduced cytoskeletal retention. Our findings reveal the importance of RNA binding for the formation of MLP assemblies, and support the emerging role of RNA as a co-factor in the organization of macromolecular complexes, with potential relevance to human disease.
